definitions.text: I don't know; who knows; search me. A complete answer on its own, and usually delivered with a shrug and downturned mouth.

examples.translation: 'When does the train arrive?' 'No idea.'

examples.text: Boh, forse domani, non si sa.
examples.translation: Who knows, maybe tomorrow, nobody's sure.

origin.etymology: Not a word so much as a conventionalised sound, and one of the first things learners notice about real Italian conversation. It communicates not just ignorance but a refusal to speculate.

definitions.text: Hmm; well now. Signals doubt, scepticism or resigned uncertainty about what has just been said.

examples.text: Mah, non ne sono così sicuro.
examples.translation: Hmm, I'm not so sure about that.
Well, we'll see.

definitions.text: Oh well; fine; whatever. Contracted from va bene, and used to accept something reluctantly or to close off a topic.

examples.translation: Fine, never mind, we'll do it tomorrow.
Come on now, don't exaggerate.

definitions.text: Come on. Encouragement, impatience or disbelief, depending entirely on intonation.
Ma dai! — 'you're kidding!' Expressing surprise.
As a softener at the end of a sentence: andiamo, dai.

examples.translation: Come on, you can do it!
No way, I don't believe it.
Come on, let's go, it's late.

definitions.text: If only! I wish. Standing alone, it expresses a wish the speaker thinks unlikely.
Maybe, perhaps. Mid-sentence it is an ordinary hedge.
With a subjunctive: even if, supposing that.
definitions.note: The standalone 'if only' sense is the one that surprises learners — it is almost the opposite of 'maybe'.

examples.translation: 'Are you going to win the lottery?' 'I wish!'
Maybe we'll see each other tomorrow.

origin.etymology: From Greek makários, 'blessed, happy' — a Byzantine borrowing that survived into Italian. The wish sense is closest to the original.

definitions.text: Cool, great. Che figo! — 'how cool!'
Of a person: attractive. Un figo, una figa in this sense.
Northern in origin; central and southern Italy say fico for the same thing.
definitions.note: Note that the feminine figa also has a vulgar anatomical sense, which is why the masculine is the safer form.

examples.translation: Your flat is so cool!

examples.text: È stato un concerto davvero figo.
examples.translation: It was a really great gig.

definitions.text: Something brilliant; a great thing. Che figata! — 'how cool is that!'

examples.text: Che figata, hanno aperto una libreria qui.
examples.translation: How great, they've opened a bookshop here.

examples.text: Il nuovo album è una figata.
examples.translation: The new album is fantastic.

definitions.text: It rocks; it's outstanding. Questo pezzo spacca — 'this track is a banger'.

examples.translation: That band is incredible live.
Your project is genuinely brilliant.

definitions.text: What a drag; how boring. An extremely common complaint about tedium rather than about anything genuinely bad.

examples.translation: Another meeting? What a drag.
This rain is so tedious.

origin.etymology: Anatomically vulgar in origin but heavily bleached — heard constantly, including from people who would not otherwise swear. Rompere le palle, 'to be a pain', comes from the same root.

definitions.text: Damn; blast. A mild curse of frustration, often extended to mannaggia a te or mannaggia la miseria.

examples.translation: Damn, I've forgotten my keys.

examples.text: Mannaggia a te e alle tue idee.
examples.translation: Damn you and your bright ideas.

origin.etymology: From Neapolitan mal ne aggia, 'may evil come of it'. Southern in origin and now thoroughly national, like a good deal of Italian informal vocabulary.

definitions.text: Damn it; bloody hell. The socially safe member of a large family of porca... expressions, the others of which are blasphemous and genuinely offensive.

examples.text: Porca miseria, si è rotto di nuovo.
examples.translation: Damn it, it's broken again.
Bloody hell it's cold!

origin.etymology: Italian swearing splits sharply between the merely vulgar and the bestemmie — blasphemies against God or the saints, which remain seriously taboo and were until recently punishable by law. porca miseria substitutes an abstract noun for the forbidden one.

definitions.text: Not to care at all. Me ne frego — 'I couldn't care less'. Chi se ne frega — 'who cares'.

examples.text: Non me ne frega niente di quello che dicono.
examples.translation: I don't care in the slightest what they say.
And who cares!

origin.etymology: Worth knowing that me ne frego was a Fascist slogan in the 1920s and 30s. The phrase long predates and outlasts that use and is entirely neutral today, but the association is still recognised by Italians.

definitions.text: To annoy, to pester. Uno scocciatore is a pest.
Reflexively, scocciarsi: to get fed up.

examples.translation: Stop pestering your sister.
I've had enough of waiting.

definitions.text: A pain in the neck; someone who will not leave you alone. The polite version of a cruder expression built on the same verb.

examples.translation: That bloke is a real pain.
Don't be such a nuisance.

definitions.text: Good luck. The conventional reply is crepi il lupo ('may the wolf die') or simply crepi — replying grazie is considered to invite bad luck.

examples.text: In bocca al lupo per l'esame!
examples.translation: Good luck with the exam!
'Good luck.' 'Thanks!'
examples.context: The exchange is fixed. Answering 'grazie' marks you as a foreigner.

origin.etymology: The logic is the same as English 'break a leg': wishing good luck directly is thought to jinx it, so you invoke the danger instead. A minority argue the wolf's mouth is protective, as a she-wolf carries her cubs — in which case crepi il lupo is a mistake. Italians argue about this.

definitions.text: That works; fair enough; it fits. Expresses that something is acceptable or reasonable.
Of a person: they're up for it. Ci sta means 'count me in'.

examples.text: Una birra dopo il lavoro? Ci sta.
examples.translation: A beer after work? Sounds good.

examples.text: Ci sta che sia in ritardo, c'è traffico.
examples.translation: It's understandable that he's late, there's traffic.

definitions.text: So; right then; well. Opens a sentence, fills a pause, calls a room to order, or introduces a conclusion. Teachers begin lessons with it and waiters begin orders with it.
At that time, as an ordinary adverb.

examples.translation: So, what are we doing tonight?
Right, everyone, quiet!

definitions.text: A euphemism for a much cruder word, used both as an exclamation and as an intensifier: che cavolo vuoi? — 'what the hell do you want?'
Non me ne importa un cavolo: I don't care at all.

examples.translation: What on earth are you doing?
Wow, what great news!

origin.etymology: Substituted for cazzo, which it resembles in shape and sound. Italian has a rich stock of such vegetable substitutions.

definitions.text: A loser; someone unlucky and uncool. Sfiga, the related noun, means bad luck.

examples.text: Che sfiga, mi si è bucata la gomma.
examples.translation: What rotten luck, I've got a flat tyre.
examples.context: sfiga on its own is about misfortune and is very mild.

examples.text: Si sente uno sfigato quando lo escludono.
examples.translation: He feels like a loser when they leave him out.

definitions.text: The overwhelming drowsiness that follows a large meal. Roman in origin, now understood nationally, and with no single-word English equivalent.

examples.text: Dopo pranzo mi viene sempre l'abbiocco.
examples.translation: I always get sleepy after lunch.
I'm unbelievably drowsy.

origin.etymology: From Roman dialect, related to a verb for a hen settling onto her eggs. The image is of sinking down and refusing to move.

definitions.text: An aperitivo with enough food laid on to replace dinner: you buy a drink and the buffet is included. A Milanese institution and a student survival strategy.

examples.translation: Shall we do an aperitivo-buffet instead of dinner?

examples.text: Dieci euro per apericena, bevuta inclusa.
examples.translation: Ten euros for the buffet aperitivo, drink included.

origin.etymology: A portmanteau of aperitivo and cena, coined in the 2000s. Purists object to both the word and the practice; neither objection has had any effect.

definitions.text: The orange aperitivo of prosecco, bitter liqueur and soda. Ordering one is the standard opening move of an Italian evening.

examples.text: Ci prendiamo uno spritz in piazza?
examples.translation: Shall we have a spritz in the square?
Two spritzes, please.

origin.etymology: From German spritzen, 'to spray' — Austrian soldiers in nineteenth-century Veneto diluted the local wine with water. The bitter liqueur came later.

definitions.text: Cunning, sly, quick to spot an angle. Admiring and disapproving at once — the furbo gets away with things, and Italians are ambivalent about whether that is a virtue.
Fare il furbo: to try it on, to game the system.

examples.text: Non fare il furbo con me.
examples.translation: Don't try it on with me.
He's too shrewd to fall for that.

origin.etymology: furbizia — the quality of being furbo — is a recurring theme in Italian self-description and satire, generally as a national failing that everyone privately admires.

definitions.text: To catch someone in the act. Mi hanno beccato — 'I got caught'.
Beccarsi: to meet up. Ci becchiamo domani — 'see you tomorrow'.

examples.translation: They caught him without a ticket.
See you at eight.

definitions.text: Cool, great. Tuscan, and a reliable regional marker — hearing it places the speaker between Florence and Livorno.

examples.translation: This place is really cool.
That's brilliant!

definitions.text: Hey; oi. The Roman attention-getter, used to open a sentence, hail a friend or express exasperation. As Roman as anything gets.

examples.translation: Oi, what are you doing?
Hey, see you later.
examples.context: Roman dialect also gives ce for ci — the two travel together.

definitions.text: So what; who cares. Roman, vulgar, and widely misused outside Rome — it expresses indifference, not admiration, and Romans will tell you so.

examples.translation: 'He's bought a new car.' 'So what.'
Who cares, what's the problem?

origin.etymology: Contracted from questi cazzi. Non-Romans frequently use it to mean 'wow, amazing', which is wrong; the correct word for that is the near-identical mecojoni.

definitions.text: Relax; take it easy; no worries. Youth slang, Roman in origin and now broadly understood.

examples.translation: Relax, we'll get there on time.
Take it easy, I'll handle it.

origin.etymology: Probably from Arabic inshallah, by way of a general Mediterranean fatalism. The derivation is plausible and not firmly established.

definitions.text: Insane, unbelievable — usually in a good sense, but usable for anything extreme.

examples.text: La vista da lassù è pazzesca.
examples.translation: The view from up there is unbelievable.
There was an insane queue.

definitions.text: Absurd — but used far more loosely than the English word, as a general marker of anything remarkable, exasperating or extreme.

examples.text: È assurdo quanto costa affittare qui.
examples.translation: It's ridiculous how much renting costs here.
Unbelievable, I can't believe it.

definitions.text: Not at all; nonsense; no chance. A flat, emphatic denial of what has just been suggested.

examples.text: —Sarà costato caro. —Macché, l'ho preso in saldo.
examples.translation: 'That must have been expensive.' 'Not at all, I got it on sale.'
Tired? Not a bit of it, I feel great.

definitions.text: You know? A tag appended to statements to check the listener is following, functioning much like English 'you know what I mean'.
Hai capito! as an exclamation of surprised admiration: 'well I never'.

examples.translation: It's a delicate matter, you know?
Well, would you look at that!

definitions.text: I mean; like. Nominally a clarifier, in practice one of the most common fillers in spoken Italian, particularly among younger speakers.

examples.text: Cioè, non è che non voglia, è che non posso.
examples.translation: I mean, it's not that I don't want to, it's that I can't.
It was, like, really strange.

definitions.text: Thank goodness; just as well. Expresses relief that something worse did not happen.

examples.translation: Thank goodness you called.

examples.text: Meno male, pensavo di averlo perso.
examples.translation: What a relief, I thought I'd lost it.

definitions.text: Like; about; sort of. A hedge and approximator: tipo alle sette, 'around seven'.
A guy, a bloke. Un tipo strano — 'an odd bloke'.

examples.translation: Let's meet around eight.

examples.text: C'era un tipo che chiedeva di te.
examples.translation: There was a guy asking for you.

definitions.text: Don't mention it; not at all. The standard reply to thanks, and to an apology.
Imagine that; as if. Sarcastically, dismissing a suggestion as obviously unlikely.

examples.translation: 'Thank you so much!' 'Don't mention it.'
As if he'd turn up on time.

definitions.text: You're welcome.
After you; please, go ahead. Holding a door, offering a seat.
What can I get you? From a waiter or shopkeeper, it is an invitation to order.
Sorry, what? Said with rising intonation, it asks for repetition.

examples.translation: 'Thanks.' 'You're welcome.'
Please, have a seat.
Sorry? I didn't catch that.

literalMeaning: What do I know of it.

definitions.text: How should I know? Also used mid-sentence as a hedge introducing an example plucked at random: 'a book, che ne so, or a plant'.

examples.text: Portagli qualcosa, che ne so, un vino.
examples.translation: Take him something, I don't know, a bottle of wine.
How am I supposed to know?

definitions.text: To rumble someone; to work out what they are really up to. Stronger than beccare — it implies seeing through a deception, not just catching someone out.

examples.translation: I saw through him straight away, he was lying.
They rumbled us.

definitions.text: To go to a lot of trouble over something. Uno sbattimento is a hassle.

examples.text: Mi sono sbattuto tutto il giorno per trovarlo.
examples.translation: I ran around all day trying to find it.
What a hassle organising all of it.

definitions.text: Guys, everyone. Clipped from ragazzi and used to address a group regardless of gender.

examples.translation: Guys, shall we get going?
Bye everyone, see you tomorrow.

definitions.text: To lose it; to flip out from stress or frustration.

examples.text: Sto per sclerare con questa stampante.
examples.translation: I'm about to lose it with this printer.

examples.text: Ha sclerato in mezzo alla riunione.
examples.translation: He lost his temper in the middle of the meeting.

origin.etymology: From sclerosi, a medical term pressed into slang service. Italian youth slang borrows from clinical vocabulary fairly often.

definitions.text: An intensified che palle — what an almighty drag.

examples.translation: This queue is an absolute nightmare.

examples.text: Che due palle, devo rifare tutto.
examples.translation: What a pain, I've got to redo the whole thing.

definitions.text: To sell out fast; to fly off the shelves.

examples.text: I biglietti sono andati a ruba.
examples.translation: The tickets sold out instantly.
That model is flying off the shelves.

definitions.text: Keep it to yourself; don't breathe a word. The image is of holding a mouthful of water so you physically cannot speak.

examples.text: È una sorpresa, acqua in bocca!
examples.translation: It's a surprise, don't say a word!

examples.text: Te lo dico, ma acqua in bocca.
examples.translation: I'll tell you, but keep it quiet.

definitions.text: There's no doubt about it. Appended to a statement to mark it as beyond argument.

examples.text: È il migliore del gruppo, non ci piove.
examples.translation: He's the best in the group, no question about it.
There's no arguing with that.

literalMeaning: To have one's hands in the dough.

definitions.text: To be involved in something, with good connections and inside knowledge. Can imply useful influence or something less savoury.

examples.text: Ha le mani in pasta in mezza città.
examples.translation: He's got a finger in every pie in half the city.

examples.text: Chiedi a lei, ha le mani in pasta.
examples.translation: Ask her, she knows how it all works.
